name: The wedding of Peleus and Thetis: Eris's golden apple
scope: The banquet that starts the whole war. T1: PELEUS, a mortal king of the Myrmidons in Phthia, marries the sea-nymph THETIS in a wedding on Mount Pelion attended by all the Olympian gods -- she is the mother, from that night on, of the child who will be ACHILLES. T2: every god and goddess is invited except ERIS, goddess of strife and discord (her name means simply 'Strife'); insulted at the exclusion, she rolls into the middle of the banquet hall a GOLDEN APPLE inscribed with a single Greek word: KALLISTEI -- 'for the fairest' (or 'to the most beautiful'). T3: THREE goddesses reach for the apple at once -- HERA, queen of the gods and wife of Zeus; ATHENA, gray-eyed goddess of wisdom and war-craft; and APHRODITE, goddess of love and desire. Each claims the apple is meant for her, and none will yield. T4: Zeus refuses to judge between his wife, his daughter, and the goddess of love -- so he sends HERMES to fetch a mortal to decide, a young man on the slopes of Mount Ida in the Troad tending sheep: PARIS, son of Priam king of Troy, exposed at birth because of a prophecy and raised as a herdsman. T5: this is why later Greek and Roman writers call the apple 'the Apple of Discord' -- the whole ten-year Trojan War, in the myth's own logic, is what an uninvited goddess and one thrown apple set in motion. Kypria fragments (a lost early poem in the Epic Cycle) preserve the setup; the story is retold at length in Apollodorus's Bibliotheke (Epitome 3.2) and in Ovid's Heroides 16. Further rungs: the Kypria says Zeus himself deliberately arranged the discord because the earth was overburdened with too many mortals; the Fates sang at the wedding, and Chiron the centaur gave Peleus a spear of ash from Pelion that only Achilles would be able to wield.
source: PRIMARY: Kypria (Cyclic epic, fragments preserved in Proclus's Chrestomathy); Apollodorus, Bibliotheke Epitome 3.2 (Peleus and Thetis wedding, Eris, the apple inscribed KALLISTEI, Hera / Athena / Aphrodite); Ovid, Heroides 16 (Paris to Helen, recounting the judgment). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the single word on the apple: KALLISTEI, 'for the fairest') and T5 (an uninvited goddess and one thrown apple started the whole ten-year war). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'apple of discord' before asking what Eris did; describe the SCENE (the sea-nymph's wedding on Mount Pelion, all the gods attending, one goddess left off the list) and let the recall be the goddess's NAME, the OBJECT she threw, or the WORD inscribed. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend from the Epic Cycle; frame as 'the Kypria says' or 'in the myth'. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Loki crashing the gods' feast in Aegir's hall -- 'the goddess of strife', 'the wedding on Mount Pelion'. history_overlap: None substantive -- pure mythology. GEOGRAPHY owns Mount Pelion in Thessaly as a place; here it is the mountaintop where the sea-nymph married the mortal king.

name: The Judgment of Paris: power, wisdom, or Helen
scope: The bribe scene that decides the war. T1: PARIS, a Trojan prince tending sheep on Mount IDA in the Troad (exposed at birth because his mother HECUBA dreamed she would bear a firebrand, raised as a herdsman by shepherds), is chosen by Zeus to judge between three goddesses claiming Eris's golden apple. T2: Hermes brings the three goddesses to him on the mountainside, and each strips before him and offers a BRIBE. HERA promises him POWER -- kingship over Asia and rule over the greatest empire of men. ATHENA promises him WISDOM AND VICTORY -- skill in war and craft such that no mortal will match him in battle. APHRODITE promises him THE MOST BEAUTIFUL WOMAN IN THE WORLD as his wife. T3: he chooses APHRODITE -- and the most beautiful woman in the world is already married. She is HELEN, daughter of Zeus and Leda (born from an egg after Zeus visited her mother as a swan), and she is the wife of MENELAUS, king of Sparta. T4: Aphrodite tells Paris that Helen is his; the other two goddesses go away shamed and furious. From that hour HERA and ATHENA are the sworn enemies of Troy in the Iliad -- Athena guides Diomedes to wound Aphrodite herself in battle (Iliad 5), and Hera repeatedly tricks Zeus to help the Greeks. Paris sails to Sparta as an ambassador, is entertained hospitably by Menelaus, and while his host is away burying his grandfather in Crete, Paris takes Helen (whether willingly, half-persuaded by Aphrodite, or by outright abduction -- Homer keeps both possibilities live) and sails home with her to Troy. T5: this is the primal 'you had to choose ONE thing and you chose the wrong one' scene of Greek myth -- Paris turned down empire and turned down wisdom for a woman, and the war that follows kills him, his brother HECTOR, and every prince of his house, and burns his city to the ground. Kypria (Cyclic epic), Apollodorus Epitome 3.2, Euripides's Trojan Women, Ovid's Heroides 16 all preserve the scene. Further rungs: the earliest hint of the judgment is in Iliad 24.29 -- Homer only glances at it, calling Paris's insult against Athena and Hera 'the folly that has come home'; some later versions have Paris also require the goddesses to strip before he will judge them.
source: PRIMARY: Iliad 24.25-30 (Homer's brief reference); Kypria fragments (preserved in Proclus's Chrestomathy); Apollodorus, Bibliotheke Epitome 3.2 (the three bribes, the choice, the abduction); Euripides, Trojan Women 924-937 (Helen recounting the judgment); Ovid, Heroides 16 (Paris's own version). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Judgment of Paris', 'Paris (mythology)', 'Helen of Troy' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the three bribes as 'power / wisdom / Helen' is the standard schema; some ancient sources list Athena's bribe as 'victory in every battle' rather than 'wisdom' -- lock 'wisdom AND victory in war' as the safe phrasing.
framing_note: The keystone Trojan War origin-ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the three bribes: POWER from Hera, WISDOM from Athena, HELEN from Aphrodite) and T5 (a shepherd prince turned down empire and wisdom for a woman and burned his own city down). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name 'Aphrodite' before asking who Paris chose; describe the SCENE (three goddesses stripping on Mount Ida, three bribes) and let the recall be WHICH goddess offered WHICH bribe, or the name of the woman he was promised. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend, layered from Kypria onward; Homer only glances at it in Iliad 24. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the tale of Ferdiad choosing to fight Cuchulainn on Queen Medb's oath -- 'the shepherd prince', 'the three goddesses on the mountain'. No 'the goddess of pure love' / etc. -- named epithets only where Homer names them ('gray-eyed Athena'). DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'three offers' scenes (Solomon's three wishes), other bribe scenes in myth, other 'exposed prince returns' scenes (Oedipus, Cyrus, Romulus), other named Trojan princes (Deiphobus, Troilus, Helenus).
history_overlap: None -- pure mythology. GEOGRAPHY owns Mount Ida as a place; here it is the mountainside where a shepherd was made a judge.

name: Helen and Paris in Troy: the muster of a thousand ships
scope: How stealing one wife becomes ten years of war. T1: HELEN, daughter of Zeus and Leda and wife of MENELAUS king of Sparta, is taken (or goes willingly, the sources disagree) with PARIS to Troy. Menelaus comes home from Crete to find his wife, and much of his palace treasure, gone. T2: before Helen ever married, so many kings and princes courted her that her stepfather TYNDAREUS was afraid of a war among the losers. On the advice of a young ODYSSEUS he made every suitor swear the OATH OF TYNDAREUS -- that whoever won her, all the others would defend that marriage against any man who tried to break it. When Menelaus calls the oath in, every king in Greece is legally sworn. T3: Menelaus goes first to his older brother AGAMEMNON, king of MYCENAE and overlord of the Achaeans (Homer's word for 'the Greeks'); Agamemnon becomes the commander of the whole expedition. Envoys are sent across Greece to summon the sworn suitors. ODYSSEUS, king of ITHACA, tries to dodge the call by pretending to be MAD -- he ploughs his own field with an ox and a donkey yoked together and sows the furrows with SALT. Palamedes exposes the trick by laying Odysseus's infant son TELEMACHUS in front of the plough; Odysseus swerves, and is drafted. T4: the fleet muster is a THOUSAND SHIPS from every corner of Greece -- Homer's Catalogue of Ships in ILIAD 2 names 29 contingents and 1,186 ships (Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus condenses it as 'the face that launched a thousand ships'). The Greek chieftains include Agamemnon of Mycenae, Menelaus of Sparta, Odysseus of Ithaca, Achilles of Phthia, Ajax the Great of Salamis, Ajax the Lesser of Locris, Diomedes of Argos, Nestor the old king of Pylos, and Idomeneus of Crete. T5: the fleet gathers at the port of AULIS in Boeotia to sail east across the Aegean -- and there, becalmed by the anger of a goddess, the expedition will pay its first terrible price before it ever reaches Troy (Iphigenia at Aulis, next topic). Further rungs: some traditions -- notably Stesichorus's Palinode and Euripides's Helen -- say the real Helen never went to Troy at all, but was carried by Hermes to EGYPT and a PHANTOM (an eidolon) fought the war in her place, and Menelaus found the real Helen there after the war (Herodotus 2.113-115 tells this Egyptian version); Homer keeps her in Troy on the walls in the Teichoscopia (Iliad 3).
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 2.494-877 (Catalogue of Ships), Iliad 3.121-244 (Helen on the walls); Apollodorus, Bibliotheke 3.10.9 (Oath of Tyndareus), Epitome 3.6-7 (Odysseus's feigned madness, the ox and donkey and salt, Palamedes and Telemachus); Herodotus 2.113-115 (Egyptian variant); Euripides, Helen (phantom-in-Troy variant); Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus V.i ('the face that launched a thousand ships'). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the ship-count in Homer is actually 1,186 -- the round 'thousand ships' is Marlowe's; frame accordingly.
framing_note: The bridge ladder from the Judgment scene to the war itself; sets up the whole cast of Achaean chieftains that later ladders will draw from. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Odysseus tries to dodge the war by ploughing his field with salt and gets caught when they lay his baby in front of the plough) and T4 ('the face that launched a thousand ships' is a phrase Homer never actually wrote -- Marlowe wrote it 2,300 years later; Homer's real number is 1,186). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem give 'oath of Tyndareus' before asking what bound the Greek kings; describe the SCENE (a wife stolen, an old oath called in, the muster at Aulis) and let the recall be who suggested the oath, who feigned madness, or how the deception was exposed. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: legendary; even if there is an archaeological Troy VIIa (destroyed c. 1180 BCE) the epic muster is legend. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the weight of the muster of the Fianna or of Charlemagne's peers -- 'the Achaeans', 'the old king of Pylos', 'the king of Ithaca'. DISTRACTOR MINE: the Achaean chieftains (Diomedes, Nestor, Idomeneus, the two Ajaxes -- all real, all wrong for 'who feigned madness'), other 'suitor oath' scenes (the suitors of Penelope, the suitors of Deianeira), other 'exposed by baby' scenes.

name: Iphigenia at Aulis: the winds refused, the deer substituted
scope: The sacrifice before the war can sail. T1: the Greek fleet is gathered at the port of AULIS in Boeotia, a thousand ships ready to cross the Aegean to Troy, but the WIND WILL NOT BLOW -- day after day the ships lie becalmed and the men grow restless. T2: the seer CALCHAS declares the cause: AGAMEMNON, the commander-in-chief, has offended the goddess ARTEMIS (in some versions by killing a sacred stag in her grove and boasting he was a better hunter than she; in others by an old family curse). The goddess will not send wind until Agamemnon sacrifices his own eldest daughter -- IPHIGENIA -- on the altar at Aulis. T3: Agamemnon sends home a letter to his wife CLYTEMNESTRA telling her to bring Iphigenia to Aulis on the pretext of a MARRIAGE -- the bridegroom, he says, will be ACHILLES. Mother and daughter come joyfully; when Achilles finds out his name has been used as bait for a killing, he swears to defend the girl. T4: in Euripides's Iphigenia at Aulis the girl at first pleads for her life and then, in one of the most famous 'change of heart' speeches in Greek tragedy, offers herself willingly -- 'I give my body to Greece. Sacrifice it, and sack Troy. This shall be my monument for ages: this is my marriage, my children, my glory' (Iphigenia at Aulis 1375-1401). She walks to the altar of her own will, veiled like a bride. T5: what happens at the altar splits the tradition. In the older AGAMEMNON of Aeschylus the knife falls and the girl dies -- 'her prayers, her cries of Father, her maiden years, / none of these the war-lords heeded' (Agamemnon 228-247), and years later Clytemnestra will kill Agamemnon in his bath for that killing. In the LATER version (Euripides, echoing an already-known variant) at the last moment ARTEMIS SUBSTITUTES a DEER on the altar and snatches Iphigenia away to Tauris (the Black Sea coast) to be her priestess -- his knife strikes the deer, not the girl. Either way the wind rises immediately and the ships sail. Further rungs: Iphigenia in Tauris (Euripides) picks up years later -- Iphigenia, now Artemis's priestess among the Taurians, is required to sacrifice every stranger who lands, and her long-lost brother ORESTES washes ashore; she saves him and they escape home with the wooden image of the goddess.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Agamemnon lures his daughter to camp with a LIE that she is to marry Achilles) and T5 (in one version the knife falls and she dies; in the other Artemis snatches her away and puts a DEER on the altar in her place). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the weight of Jephthah and his daughter in Judges 11, or of Abraham and Isaac on Mount Moriah -- 'the commander', 'the daughter', 'the seer'. No editorializing about ancient cruelty. history_overlap: None. GEOGRAPHY owns Aulis as a place; here it is the harbour where the wind would not blow.

name: Achilles among the daughters of Lycomedes: the merchant's trick
scope: How Odysseus fetches the boy the war cannot start without. T1: THETIS, the sea-nymph mother of ACHILLES, knows from prophecy that her son has TWO possible fates -- if he stays home he will live a long quiet unremembered life; if he goes to Troy his name will be sung forever but he will die young. She hides him at the court of King LYCOMEDES on the island of SKYROS, dressed as a GIRL and living among the king's daughters. T2: he takes a girl's name -- PYRRHA, 'red-haired' -- and while he is there fathers a son on the princess DEIDAMEIA (that son will be NEOPTOLEMUS, who fights at Troy in the war's last year). T3: the seer CALCHAS tells the Greek chieftains that Troy cannot fall without Achilles. ODYSSEUS is sent to Skyros to find and fetch him. Disguised as a travelling MERCHANT, Odysseus lays out his wares in the palace courtyard for the king's daughters to admire -- bright cloths, jewels, mirrors, ribbons -- and hidden among the pretty things a SHIELD and a SPEAR. T4: the girls crowd around the cloth and the jewels; one of them ignores all of it and reaches straight for the WEAPONS. Some versions add a further trick: while the 'girl' is examining the spear, Odysseus's men outside the courtyard sound a WAR-TRUMPET (a war-cry, or a mock alarm of pirates), and only one 'daughter' snatches up the shield and stands ready to fight. That is Achilles. He is unmasked, and cannot deny it. T5: he agrees to sail -- knowing what he is choosing. The fate his mother tried to hide him from is now on him: to Troy, and to a name that will still be sung 3,000 years later, and to an early death by an arrow. The scene is not in Homer's Iliad (Homer just names Achilles at Troy) -- it is developed in the Cyclic epics (Kypria) and told in full by Statius in his 1st-century Latin Achilleid, by Apollodorus (Epitome 3.13-14) and by Ovid (Metamorphoses 13.162-170, from Odysseus's own boastful mouth). Further rungs: the name PYRRHA ('red-haired') is why Achilles's son by Deidameia is later called PYRRHUS as well as NEOPTOLEMUS ('new to war'); Skyros in the northern Aegean is a real island (the poet Rupert Brooke is buried there); some vase-paintings show Achilles being unmasked with the trumpet-blast rather than the shield-reach.

name: The shield of Achilles: the world Hephaestus hammered
scope: The most famous piece of armour in Greek literature. T1: PATROCLUS, Achilles's dearest companion, has been killed by HECTOR while wearing Achilles's own armour (Iliad 16); Hector has stripped that armour from his body. Achilles has nothing to fight in. His mother THETIS goes down to the sea-forge of HEPHAESTUS, the smith-god of the Olympians, and asks him to make her son NEW armour. T2: Hephaestus works all night. He hammers out for Achilles a HELMET, a CORSELET, a set of GREAVES made of tin, and above all a SHIELD -- and on the shield he lays out the whole world in five layers of metal (bronze, tin, gold, silver, and one more) in scene after scene of inlaid figures. T3: this is the EKPHRASIS of Iliad 18.478-608 -- one of the oldest and most famous set-piece descriptions in Western literature. On the shield there is: EARTH, SKY, SEA, the SUN, the FULL MOON, and 'all the constellations that garland the heavens, the Pleiades and Hyades and the mighty strength of Orion and the Bear, whom men also call the Wain' (Iliad 18.485-489, Lattimore). T4: two cities are inlaid next -- a CITY AT PEACE (with a wedding-procession by torchlight and a lawsuit in the market where two men argue over the blood-price of a killing) and a CITY AT WAR (besieged, with an ambush at the river). Then farming scenes: PLOUGHING (Iliad 18.541), HARVEST (550), GRAPE-PICKING (561), OXEN attacked by TWO LIONS (573), a SHEEP-PASTURE, and a great DANCING-FLOOR like the one Daedalus made for Ariadne at Knossos (590). T5: around the very rim runs the RIVER OF OCEAN -- Okeanos, the great world-encircling river Homer names the boundary of everything. The whole cosmos is hammered on one shield. Auden's 1952 poem 'The Shield of Achilles' is a modern answering-poem to this passage. Further rungs: when Achilles first straps on the new armour, he tests it -- 'the arms became like WINGS' (Iliad 19.386, Lattimore) and lift him -- an image reused by every later 'hero's new armour' scene in Western literature; the ekphrasis in Virgil's Aeneid 8 (the shield of Aeneas by the same god Hephaestus, called Vulcan in Latin) is a deliberate answering-piece 800 years later.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 18.478-608 (the full ekphrasis of the shield); Iliad 18.369-467 (Thetis at the forge, Hephaestus's welcome); Iliad 19.369-391 (Achilles strapping on the armour, 'like wings'); Virgil, Aeneid 8.626-731 (Vulcan's answering shield of Aeneas). Translations: Richmond Lattimore (Chicago 1951) is the standard scholarly English; Robert Fagles (Penguin 1990) the popular. history_overlap: None -- pure text.

name: The wrath of Achilles and the death of Patroclus
scope: The engine of the Iliad. T1: the first word of the Iliad is MENIN -- 'wrath' -- 'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus, and its devastation, which put pains thousandfold upon the Achaeans' (Iliad 1.1-2, Lattimore). AGAMEMNON has forced Achilles to give up the captive girl BRISEIS to replace his own captive Chryseis (whose father, the priest of Apollo, has been sending plague on the camp). Achilles WITHDRAWS from the war -- he will not fight, and his mother Thetis persuades Zeus to let the Trojans push the Greeks back to their ships to teach Agamemnon a lesson. T2: the Trojans, led by HECTOR, Priam's eldest son, press the Greeks all the way to the beach and set fire to the first ship (Iliad 15). PATROCLUS, Achilles's oldest and dearest companion (raised with him in Peleus's house), begs Achilles at least to let him go into battle wearing Achilles's armour, so the Trojans will think Achilles has returned. T3: Achilles agrees but warns him -- push the Trojans back from the ships, then STOP; do not chase them under the walls of Troy. Patroclus disobeys, presses them all the way to the Scaean Gates, and there APOLLO himself strikes him -- 'Patroclus was left to die, undone by godhead and Euphorbos and the spear of Hector' (Iliad 16). Hector delivers the killing blow. T4: word reaches Achilles. He collapses in the dust and pours black ashes on his golden hair, howling so loud that his mother hears him under the sea and comes up to him. Antilochus holds his hands to keep him from cutting his own throat. His wrath, which had been aimed at Agamemnon, now turns fully on HECTOR -- and he swears he will not eat, will not sleep, will not bury Patroclus, until Hector is dead by his hand. He and Agamemnon are RECONCILED in front of the whole camp. T5: he goes back into battle in the new armour Hephaestus has forged him (the shield of the previous topic). The war has changed shape. What began as 'Agamemnon insulted me' is now 'the man I loved is dead' -- and it will not end until Achilles kills Hector, and until Achilles himself is dead. Further rungs: the RELATIONSHIP between Achilles and Patroclus is described as HETAIROS ('companion') in Homer; later Greek writers, most famously Aeschylus in his lost Myrmidons and Plato in the Symposium 179e-180a, take the relationship as a lover-and-beloved -- the Iliad itself keeps it as an intense sworn friendship. CHRYSES the priest, his daughter Chryseis, Apollo's plague-arrows on the camp: the setup of book 1.

Lattimore (Chicago 1951) and Fagles (Penguin 1990) standard English translations. Aeschylus, Myrmidons (fragments); Plato, Symposium 179e-180a (Achilles-and-Patroclus as lovers, a later reading). Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the whole 15,000-line epic OPENS with the single word 'wrath' -- MENIN) and T3-T4 (Patroclus's death is what actually gets Achilles back into the war -- his fight was never really with Agamemnon in the end). name: Achilles drags Hector round the walls of Troy
scope: The killing of Hector and its terrible aftermath. T1: HECTOR, Priam's eldest son and the greatest fighter of Troy, waits alone outside the SCAEAN GATE for ACHILLES to come. His father Priam and his mother Hecuba both beg him from the wall to come inside; his wife ANDROMACHE and their baby son ASTYANAX are already inside. Hector refuses to run. T2: when Achilles finally comes on him, gleaming in the new god-forged armour, Hector's nerve breaks and he RUNS. Achilles chases him THREE TIMES around the walls of Troy -- 'as when a hawk in the mountains, the swiftest of winged things, swoops on a trembling dove' (Iliad 22.139-142, Lattimore). Zeus in heaven weighs their two fates in his golden scales, and Hector's sinks. Athena in the shape of Hector's brother DEIPHOBUS deceives him into stopping to make his stand. T3: the fight is short. Achilles knows every joint of his own armour that Hector is now wearing, and drives his spear into the one gap AT HECTOR'S THROAT (Iliad 22.324-329). Hector, dying, begs Achilles to accept ransom for his body from Priam so his people can bury him. Achilles refuses -- 'I wish only that my rage, my fury, would drive me now to hack your flesh away and eat you raw' (Iliad 22.346-347, Fagles). Hector prophesies with his last breath that PARIS and APOLLO will kill Achilles at the same Scaean Gate. T4: Achilles pierces Hector's ANKLE-TENDONS behind the heel, runs oxhide THONGS through them, and TIES the body to the back of his CHARIOT. He drags the corpse behind the horses THREE TIMES around the walls in full view of Priam, Hecuba, and Andromache on the ramparts (Iliad 22.395-405). Andromache faints. Every day for TWELVE DAYS after that, Achilles hitches the body up again and drags it round Patroclus's burial-mound (Iliad 24.14-18). T5: Apollo protects the body throughout -- keeping the skin unbroken, wrapping it in a golden aegis so the sun and the dust and the dragging cannot mar it (Iliad 24.20-21). The gods on Olympus grow angry with Achilles's excess; Zeus decides Hector must be ransomed. That decision sets up the last book of the Iliad -- Priam's night visit to Achilles's tent (next topic). Further rungs: Hector's earlier farewell to Andromache and Astyanax at the Scaean Gate (Iliad 6.390-502) is one of the tenderest scenes in Homer -- the baby cries at his father's terrifying helmet-plume, and Hector takes the helmet off and laughs; that farewell is the emotional weight the death-scene later cashes in.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 22 (whole book; Hector at the gate, the three-times chase, Zeus's scales, Athena as Deiphobus, spear at the throat, the thongs and chariot, Andromache fainting); Iliad 24.1-21 (the twelve days of dragging round Patroclus's tomb, Apollo protecting the body); Iliad 6.390-502 (the earlier farewell to Andromache and Astyanax). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hector', 'Achilles', 'Iliad' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'I wish only that my rage' (Achilles refusing ransom in book 22) -- verify Fagles's exact wording.
framing_note: The two-scene ladder -- the killing itself, then the DRAGGING that shocks even the gods. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Achilles ties the body to his chariot and DRAGS it round the walls of Troy three times IN FRONT of the man's wife and mother -- then does it every day for twelve more days) and T2 (the chase itself is three times around the walls, and Hector's nerve breaks and he runs). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'chariot' or 'behind the horses' before asking what Achilles did with Hector's body; describe the SCENE (a duel at the gate, a spear at the throat, a dying request for ransom, a father and wife watching from the wall) and let the recall be the specific place of the spear-wound, the number of times round the walls, or what Achilles did with the body after the kill. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the flyting and killing of Ferdiad by Cuchulainn at the ford -- 'the eldest son of Priam', 'the Scaean Gate'. Do NOT soften Achilles's cruelty -- the passage does not soften it. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Iliad duels (Menelaus and Paris in book 3, Ajax and Hector in book 7 -- both left alive), other 'dragged behind chariot' images (Actaeon torn by his own dogs -- different), other body-mutilation scenes (Deiphobus at the sack, later).
history_overlap: None -- pure Homer.

name: Priam in the tent of Achilles: 'I have kissed the hand'
scope: The last book of the Iliad, and one of the deepest scenes in Homer. T1: PRIAM, the aged king of Troy, has watched from the walls as ACHILLES killed his son HECTOR and dragged the body round the walls behind his chariot. Twelve days later Hector's corpse is still lying in the Greek camp, still un-buried, and the gods on Olympus have decided this cannot stand. Zeus sends IRIS the messenger down to Priam: he must go, alone at night, into the enemy camp with ransom, and beg for his son's body. T2: guided by HERMES in the shape of a young Greek captain, the old king crosses no-man's-land at midnight in a wagon loaded with treasure and enters Achilles's tent. He clasps Achilles's knees in the ritual gesture of the SUPPLIANT and KISSES the hand of the man who killed his son. T3: 'Remember your own father,' Priam says, 'a man as old as I am, at home in Phthia. Now think of me -- I have endured what no man on earth has ever endured before, I have put my lips to the hands of the man who killed my son' (Iliad 24.503-506, Fagles, closely). T4: Achilles weeps -- for his own father PELEUS whom he will never see again, and for PATROCLUS. Priam weeps for Hector. The two enemies sit together in the tent and cry, then eat a meal together, and Achilles marvels at how god-like the old king still looks even in his grief. T5: Achilles agrees. He grants a TRUCE of ELEVEN DAYS for the funeral -- nine to cut wood for the pyre, one for the burning, one for the mound -- and himself has Hector's body washed, anointed, and laid gently in the wagon so that Priam will not have to see how it has been treated (Iliad 24.582-591). The whole Iliad, which opened on the word 'wrath' and ran for 15,000 lines on killing, ENDS with 'and so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses' (Iliad 24.804, the poem's last line). Further rungs: HERMES's disguise as the young Myrmidon warrior is the god's only appearance in the Iliad guiding a mortal in body-shape rather than voice; the ELEVEN-day truce is one of the very few pauses in the war; the funeral games for Hector are outside the poem but referenced.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 24 (whole book; Iris to Priam, Hermes as guide, the crossing at night, the supplication, 'remember your own father' 486-502, 'I have kissed the hand' 503-506, Achilles weeping for Peleus, the eleven-day truce 660-670, the poem's closing line 804). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Iliad', 'Priam' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 'kissed the hand' line -- lock the Fagles translation ('I have put my lips to the hands of the man who killed my son'); Lattimore has 'I have gathered to my lips the hands of the man who has slain my children'. Both are usable; pick one per rung.
framing_note: The emotional CLIMAX ladder of the whole Iliad -- the moment that changes what the war has meant. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the OLD KING sneaks into the enemy camp at night and KISSES the hand of the man who killed his son) and T5 (the Iliad, which begins on the word 'wrath', ends with 'and so the Trojans buried Hector, breaker of horses'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem contain the phrase 'kissed the hand' before asking what Priam did; describe the SCENE (an old king in an enemy tent at night, a wagon of ransom, the corpse of a son) and let the recall be the exact GESTURE, the RANSOM given, or the DURATION of the truce granted. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer -- and generally regarded (Aristotle, Simone Weil, George Steiner) as one of the greatest scenes in all of Western literature. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as David weeping over Absalom, or Priam's answering-scene in Vergil's Aeneid where he dies at the altar in the sack -- 'the old king', 'the young killer', 'the tent at night'. No 'noble pagan grief', no ornament. DISTRACTOR MINE: other supplication-in-tent scenes (Odysseus at Circe's house, the embassy to Achilles in Iliad 9), other 'ransom for the body' scenes.
history_overlap: None -- pure Homer.

name: Achilles's heel: the arrow, the Styx, and Thetis's grip
scope: How the greatest warrior of the Greeks dies. T1: at the birth of ACHILLES, his mother THETIS was told that he would die young in battle. To try to save him, she dipped the newborn baby in the waters of the RIVER STYX, the river of the underworld, whose waters made a body invulnerable. T2: she held him by his HEEL as she dipped him -- and that heel, gripped in her fingers, never touched the water. Everywhere else on his body a weapon could not cut him; his heel was the one place a weapon could. This is why every language in the West has the phrase 'AN ACHILLES HEEL' for the single vulnerable spot in something otherwise proof. T3: at Troy, in the tenth year of the war, after killing Hector and many others, Achilles goes into battle near the SCAEAN GATE. PARIS -- the man who started the war by taking Helen, who has done little else in ten years but hide behind his brother Hector -- takes up a BOW and shoots. APOLLO GUIDES the arrow. T4: the arrow strikes Achilles in the HEEL (in some late versions the ankle, in older versions unspecified) and he falls, and dies. His body is fought over -- AJAX THE GREAT carries the corpse off the field while ODYSSEUS holds off the Trojans covering the retreat (this is where the later contest for Achilles's armour begins). T5: the STYX-dipping story of the heel is NOT in Homer -- Homer only says Achilles died to a shaft that Paris shot with Apollo's help (Iliad 22.359-360, Hector's dying prophecy). The dip in the Styx and the mother's grip on the heel first appear in Statius's Achilleid (1st c. CE) and in fuller form in a scholium; the medieval and modern 'Achilles heel' is the developed version. Further rungs: an alternative ancient tradition (Aeschylus, lost play Nereids; Ptolemy Chennus) says he was made invulnerable not by the Styx dip but by being anointed with fire by Thetis when he was a baby -- with the same result at the heel; the KEY word HEEL in Greek is PTERNA (from which 'pternic-' cognates come).
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 22.359-360 (Hector's dying prophecy that Apollo and Paris will kill Achilles at the Scaean Gate) and Odyssey 24.36-42 (a shade recounting Achilles's death and burial); Statius, Achilleid 1.269-270 (Thetis dipping the child in the Styx, holding him by the heel); Servius's commentary on Aeneid 6.57 (heel version); Apollodorus, Bibliotheke Epitome 5.3 (Paris shoots, Apollo guides). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Achilles heel', 'Achilles' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia 'Achilles', 'Achilles' heel'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: state the Statius / Servius attribution honestly -- the heel-dip is post-Homeric.
framing_note: The one 'vulnerable spot' ladder in Greek myth (Balder's mistletoe is its Norse sibling; both are worth noting cross-tradition in later thematic ladders). Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his own MOTHER made him invulnerable but she was holding him by the heel while she did it, so the heel is the ONE spot she couldn't dip) and T3 (of all the great warriors who could have killed him it's PARIS -- who has done almost nothing in the war -- with Apollo guiding the shot). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'heel' before asking where his weak spot was; describe the SCENE (a mother trying to save a child, an underworld river, a mother's grip) and let the recall be the RIVER, the BODY-PART held, or the WEAPON that killed him. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend, and specifically POST-HOMERIC in its most famous form (Statius) -- the ladder must be honest that Homer doesn't tell the heel story, only the arrow. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Balder made invulnerable to everything except mistletoe, or Sigurd's one shoulder-blade the dragon-blood missed -- 'the sea-nymph mother', 'the one spot she could not cover'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other invulnerable heroes (Ajax the Great made invulnerable except the armpit, in some versions; Balder except mistletoe; Sigurd except one shoulder-blade), other 'shot by an arrow' famous deaths (Harold at Hastings -- history bank, but a real distractor), other rivers of the underworld (Lethe, Acheron, Cocytus, Phlegethon).
history_overlap: None. Note thematic overlap with Balder / mistletoe (Norse strand) for the invulnerable-with-one-weak-spot pattern -- keep specifics distinct.

name: The madness of Ajax: slaughtering sheep for generals
scope: The most famous post-Achilles Greek tragedy. T1: after Achilles's death the ARMOUR of Achilles (the god-forged shield and the rest, made by Hephaestus) is not to be inherited -- the Greek chieftains vote to decide who deserves it. The two contenders are AJAX THE GREAT (Ajax son of Telamon, king of Salamis, the strongest fighter left in the camp -- the man who carried Achilles's body off the field) and ODYSSEUS. T2: the vote is rigged, or so Ajax believes -- ODYSSEUS wins the armour with his cleverness of speech; Ajax, who saved the body, gets nothing. He is publicly shamed in front of the whole army. That night his mind breaks. T3: he takes up his sword and goes out to KILL AGAMEMNON and MENELAUS and ODYSSEUS for the insult. But ATHENA, who is Odysseus's protector, casts a MADNESS on him -- so that he sees the Greek chieftains and instead attacks the CATTLE and the SHEEP of the camp herds. In the darkness he slaughters them one by one, thinking he is butchering his enemies; he drags a huge RAM back to his tent and TIES it to a post, mistaking it for Odysseus, and begins whipping it with a cord. T4: at dawn Athena lifts the madness. Ajax sees what he has done. He is surrounded by carcasses; his hands are bloody with sheep-blood; the ram at the tent-post is bawling. In Sophocles's tragedy AJAX (composed c. 440s BCE), his captive concubine TECMESSA and his infant son EURYSACES ('Broad-Shield', named for his father's famous seven-hide shield) find him weeping among the corpses. He tells them all to leave. T5: alone at last, he plants the HILT of his SWORD in the earth on the seashore, points the blade upward, and RUNS ONTO IT with the whole weight of his body. This is the death that gives us the phrase 'to fall on one's sword' in English. His half-brother TEUCER later has to fight Agamemnon and Menelaus for the right even to bury him. Further rungs: Ajax's SHIELD in Homer is described as 'like a tower, of seven ox-hides with an eighth layer of bronze on top' (Iliad 7.219-220) -- the reason his son is called Eurysaces, 'broad-shield'; when Odysseus later meets Ajax's SHADE in Hades (Odyssey 11.541-565) he tries to make peace, but Ajax turns his back and walks away in silence -- one of the most famous moments of dignified fury in Greek literature.
source: PRIMARY: Sophocles, Ajax (whole play, esp. 91-133 the madness on the flocks, 815-865 the sword-planting monologue and death); Odyssey 11.541-565 (Ajax's silent shade in the underworld); Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.1-398 (the whole contest for the arms between Ajax and Odysseus). Little Iliad and Aithiopis fragments (Cyclic epics) preserve the earliest form. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Ajax the Great', 'Ajax (Sophocles)' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'seven-hide shield' of Ajax -- verify Iliad 7.219 wording; 'Broad-Shield' translation of Eurysaces.
framing_note: The bridge ladder between the Iliad and the Nostoi (homecomings) -- teaches the post-Achilles collapse of the Achaean camp. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Athena drives him MAD so that instead of killing the Greek generals he slaughters the CAMP SHEEP thinking they are the generals, and drags a RAM back to his tent to whip thinking it's Odysseus) and T5 (he plants his own sword blade-up in the sand and RUNS ON IT -- the origin of 'to fall on one's sword'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'sheep' before asking what Ajax attacked in his madness; describe the SCENE (the vote for the dead man's armour, the shamed loser, the night raid on the camp) and let the recall be WHAT he actually killed, WHO was inside the ram, or HOW he ended his own life. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend, primary text is Sophocles's tragedy of that name. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Saul falling on his own sword on Gilboa (1 Samuel 31) or Cuchulainn tying himself to a stone to die standing -- 'the strongest fighter left', 'the shamed loser'. DISTRACTOR MINE: the OTHER Ajax (Ajax the Lesser, of Locris, who drags Cassandra from Athena's altar and dies at sea for it -- must be distinguished by CITY / SIZE), other madness-driven-killings (Hercules killing his own children under Hera's madness), other 'fall on the sword' deaths (Saul, Brutus, Cato the Younger -- history-adjacent).
history_overlap: None.

name: The Trojan Horse: Odysseus's stratagem and Sinon's tears
scope: The most famous trick in Western literature. T1: after ten years of siege the walls of Troy are still unbroken; the Greeks cannot take the city by force. ODYSSEUS proposes a trick. Under his direction the Greek craftsman EPEIOS builds a huge HOLLOW WOODEN HORSE, big enough to hide picked warriors inside, with the goddess ATHENA's help -- and an inscription on its flank dedicating it to Athena. The rest of the Greek army breaks camp and pretends to sail away, hiding their fleet behind the island of TENEDOS just off the coast. T2: the Trojans wake to find the beach empty except for the horse. Debate breaks out. The old priest of Apollo, LAOCOON, is deeply suspicious -- 'I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts' (Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes, Virgil, Aeneid 2.49; the English 'beware Greeks bearing gifts' is a loose paraphrase). He hurls his spear into the horse's flank and the wood BOOMS hollow. T3: a Greek prisoner is dragged in -- SINON, who has apparently been left behind. Sinon weeps and swears he was to be sacrificed by his own side (as Iphigenia once was) and escaped, and that the horse is a peace-offering to Athena to buy safe passage home. If the Trojans burn it, Athena will destroy them; if they drag it inside their walls, the Greeks can never conquer Troy. Priam takes pity on him and cuts him loose. T4: at that moment TWO enormous SERPENTS come out of the sea from Tenedos, coil themselves around Laocoon and his TWO SONS on the beach, and crush and devour all three (the scene captured in the famous LAOCOON GROUP marble now in the Vatican, c. 1st c. BCE). The Trojans read this as proof that Laocoon was wrong and Sinon was right; they cut a breach in their own wall to drag the horse inside. Cassandra prophesies disaster and no one listens. T5: that night, while the Trojans feast and sleep, Sinon lights a beacon on the wall to signal the fleet behind Tenedos, and Odysseus and his men climb DOWN a rope-ladder from a trapdoor in the horse's belly. They open the gates from inside; the Greek army pours in; Troy burns. The horse itself is not in the Iliad (which ends before it) -- it is told at length in ODYSSEY 8 (the bard Demodocus sings it at Alcinous's court), OVID and above all VIRGIL's AENEID 2, in Aeneas's own eyewitness voice. Further rungs: named warriors inside the horse (Odysseus, Menelaus, Diomedes, Neoptolemus son of Achilles, and Epeios the builder who was so afraid he needed help down); Helen walks around the horse at night calling out to the men inside in the voices of their wives, trying to trick them into answering, and Odysseus has to physically hold hands over their mouths (Odyssey 4.271-289).
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 4.271-289 (Helen's trick calling the wives' voices) and 8.499-520 (Demodocus sings the horse in Alcinous's court); Virgil, Aeneid 2 (whole book, Aeneas's own eyewitness account, esp. 2.13-56 Laocoon, 2.49 'Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes', 2.199-227 the serpents, 2.256-267 the fleet returning and men descending); Apollodorus, Epitome 5.14-19; Little Iliad and Iliou Persis fragments (Cyclic epics). The Laocoon marble group is Roman-copy Hellenistic sculpture c. 1st c. BCE, now Vatican Museums. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'wooden horse' before asking how Troy fell; describe the SCENE (a ten-year siege, an empty beach, a lone Greek prisoner in tears, a suspicious old priest, huge sea-serpents from Tenedos) and let the recall be the ANIMAL the horse was, the PRISONER who lied, or the fate of LAOCOON. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend; not in the Iliad (which ends earlier); primary sources are Odyssey 8, Virgil's Aeneid 2, and the Cyclic Little Iliad / Iliou Persis fragments. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as any classic strategy-trick story -- Robin at the Sheriff's tournament, Loki bringing Idunn back in a nut, Cuchulainn's champion's portion. 'The craftsman Epeios', 'the old priest of Apollo', 'the Greek prisoner in tears'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Odysseus tricks (the Cyclops's 'Nobody' -- adjacent-real and in this strand), other 'trick to take a city' stories (Gideon's torches in Judges 7 -- Christian-strand distractor honest), other named Trojan seers (Cassandra, Helenus, Laocoon).

name: The sack of Troy: Cassandra at the altar, Astyanax from the walls
scope: The night the city burned. T1: after the Trojan Horse is dragged inside the walls at nightfall (previous topic), the Greek warriors climb down from its belly, open the SCAEAN GATE from within, and the Greek army pours back into the city from the fleet hidden behind Tenedos. Troy is torched. King PRIAM is cut down at his household altar by NEOPTOLEMUS (Achilles's son), who kills first Priam's son POLITES in front of him and then the old king himself, gray hair pulled back, throat on his own altar (Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558). T2: CASSANDRA, Priam's prophet-daughter -- cursed by Apollo to always speak the truth and never be believed -- flees to the temple of ATHENA on the citadel and clings to the WOODEN CULT IMAGE of the goddess for sanctuary. AJAX THE LESSER (Ajax son of Oileus of Locris, NOT the great Ajax who has already killed himself) drags her away from the altar so violently that the wooden image of Athena is dislodged and topples. The sacrilege is what makes Athena, up until now on the Greek side, turn against the returning fleet -- most of the storms and shipwrecks of the Nostoi begin here. T3: HECTOR's baby son ASTYANAX (the child who cried at his father's helmet-plume in Iliad 6) is a problem. If he grows up he will avenge his father. In the Iliou Persis, in Euripides's Trojan Women, and in the Little Iliad, ODYSSEUS argues (or in one variant, NEOPTOLEMUS carries out) that the child must die. The Greeks throw ASTYANAX from the walls of Troy to his death (Trojan Women 719-739, 1133-1206 -- his broken body is later brought back on his father's own great shield for burial). T4: HECUBA, Priam's queen, is enslaved to Odysseus; ANDROMACHE, Hector's widow, to Neoptolemus (who has just killed her father-in-law and her son); CASSANDRA to Agamemnon (who will bring her home to Mycenae where his wife Clytemnestra will kill them both in the bath); POLYXENA, Priam's youngest daughter, is sacrificed on Achilles's tomb to give his shade a bride. The temple treasures of Troy are looted; the city is burnt to the ground. T5: the moral shock -- especially the killing of the child and the dragging from the altar -- turns even Greek storytellers against the victors. In Euripides's Trojan Women (staged in Athens in 415 BCE during Athens's own war with Melos, and often read as a protest against it), the war looks less like a triumph and more like an atrocity. The gods themselves, in the play's prologue, plan the storms that will scatter the Greek fleet on the way home. Further rungs: Cassandra's earlier curse -- Apollo gave her prophecy in exchange for her promised love, and when she refused him, he could not take the gift back but added the curse that no one would ever believe her; she foretold the horse and no one listened.
source: PRIMARY: Virgil, Aeneid 2.437-566 (the sack, Priam killed at the altar with Polites); Euripides, Trojan Women (whole play, esp. 240-292 the enslavement lots, 709-779 and 1133-1206 Astyanax hurled from the walls); Euripides, Hecuba (Polyxena's sacrifice); Apollodorus, Epitome 5.20-25; Iliou Persis fragments (Cyclic epic); Odyssey 8.514-520 (Demodocus's song of the sack). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sack of Troy', 'Cassandra', 'Astyanax', 'Ajax the Lesser' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the sacrilege that turned Athena against the Greeks (Ajax the Lesser and Cassandra) is a critical fact for the coming Odyssey ladder; make sure the two Ajaxes are visibly distinguished.
framing_note: The dark counterweight to the Trojan Horse cleverness -- what the trick actually leads to. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (they throw HECTOR's baby son from the walls of Troy -- the same baby who cried at his father's helmet-plume in the earlier scene -- because if he grows up he will avenge his father) and T2 (Cassandra, the prophet-daughter, is DRAGGED FROM THE ALTAR of Athena by Ajax the Lesser, and THAT sacrilege is why Athena turns on the Greek fleet on the way home). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name 'Astyanax' before asking what the Greeks did with Hector's son; describe the SCENE (a burning city, a temple altar, a young mother, a baby) and let the recall be the specific ACT (thrown from the walls), the specific PLACE (temple of Athena) or the specific PERPETRATOR (Ajax the Lesser vs Neoptolemus). HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure legend from the Iliou Persis / Aeneid / Euripides. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the sack of Jerusalem in Josephus, or the sack of Lindisfarne in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle -- the specifics are grim and Euripides doesn't soften them, so the ladder shouldn't either. No editorializing about pagan savagery. DISTRACTOR MINE: the TWO Ajaxes (Great vs Lesser, easy to confuse -- pin the roles), the FATE of each Trojan royal woman (Hecuba to Odysseus, Andromache to Neoptolemus, Cassandra to Agamemnon, Polyxena on the tomb -- distractor mine of pairings), other 'child of the enemy killed for succession' scenes (the massacre of Athaliah's grandchildren, Herod at Bethlehem -- Christian-strand distractor).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the archaeology of Troy VIIa's burnt destruction layer c. 1180 BCE; theology owns the STORIES of the sack.

name: Aeneas fleeing Troy: father on his back, son by the hand
scope: The founding-image of Rome. T1: AENEAS, son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the goddess Aphrodite (Venus in Latin), a Trojan warrior of the royal line but NOT of Priam's immediate family, is inside the city on the night Troy falls. He has fought all night trying to hold the citadel; his goddess-mother appears to him and warns him the city is doomed -- staying to die there will change nothing; he must GET OUT and carry the future of Troy with him. T2: he goes home. His father ANCHISES is old and lame and refuses to leave. Aeneas cannot carry him against his will. Then a lambent FLAME plays around the head of Aeneas's young son ASCANIUS (also called IULUS in Roman tradition, the ancestor from whom the Julian family -- Julius Caesar, Augustus -- claim descent) without burning him, and a shooting star crosses the sky. Anchises reads the sign and agrees. T3: Aeneas HOISTS the old man ONTO HIS BACK -- with the household gods, the PENATES of Troy, in Anchises's arms -- takes his son ASCANIUS BY THE HAND, and leaves the burning city on foot. His wife CREUSA follows behind him. T4: in the dark and the smoke Creusa becomes separated from them and is lost. Aeneas rushes back into the burning city looking for her; her ghost appears to him and tells him she is dead, and that a new wife and a new kingdom in a western land await him -- go on without her (Aeneid 2.771-795). T5: Aeneas gathers other Trojan survivors on Mount IDA outside the city and sets sail on a wandering that will echo the Odyssey -- Delos, Crete, the Strophades, Buthrotum, Sicily, Carthage (where Dido will fall in love with him), and finally the mouth of the TIBER in Italy. His descendants (through Ascanius and, generations later, Romulus) will found ROME. The father-on-the-back scene is one of the most-painted images of the Aeneid; Bernini's marble group AENEAS, ANCHISES, AND ASCANIUS (Villa Borghese, 1618-1619) shows all three generations in a single upright column. Further rungs: the household gods carried out of Troy -- the PENATES -- are why later Roman religion has a state cult of the Penates of the Roman people, thought of as the same objects Aeneas carried from Troy; the ATRIUM in a Roman house has a small shrine for them; Julius Caesar and Augustus explicitly traced their family (the gens Julia) back to Iulus / Ascanius.
source: PRIMARY: Virgil, Aeneid 2.634-804 (whole flight sequence -- Venus's warning, Anchises's refusal, the flame on Ascanius, hoisting Anchises, taking Ascanius by the hand, Creusa lost and her ghost); Aeneid 1-6 (the wanderings and Dido); Aeneid 7-12 (the war in Italy). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Aeneas', 'Anchises', 'Ascanius' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia 'Aeneas', 'Aeneid'. Also relevant: Bernini's marble group 'Aeneas, Anchises, and Ascanius' (Villa Borghese, Rome, 1618-1619). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the Penates story links Trojan household gods to Roman state religion -- verify Aeneid 2.717 wording ('sacra suosque tibi commendo penates') and lock as the moment Anchises takes the gods.
framing_note: The bridge ladder from Troy to Rome; the archetypal 'three generations at once' image (grandfather / father / son) of Western literature. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Aeneas carries his OLD FATHER on his BACK, holds his YOUNG SON by the HAND, and leaves the burning city -- three generations in one frame) and T4 (his wife CREUSA is lost in the smoke and her GHOST tells him to go on without her). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'on his back' before asking how Aeneas carried his father out; describe the SCENE (a burning city, an old lame father who won't leave, a small son, a wife somewhere behind) and let the recall be WHO he was carrying, WHO was holding his hand, or WHAT was in the father's arms (the household gods). HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: legend; Aeneid is Virgil's 1st-c. BCE poem building the Roman national epic on Homeric bones. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same voice one would use for Lot leaving Sodom, or Noah loading the ark -- 'the old father', 'the small son', 'the burning city'. No 'the pious Aeneas' pomp -- Virgil calls him 'pius Aeneas' but the epithet doesn't need to be quoted in a kid stem. DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'father on back' images (Simeon carrying the Christ child, John the Baptist carried by his mother -- close but wrong), other Trojan survivors (Antenor -- also said to have escaped, founded Padua in one tradition), other 'lost wife' scenes (Orpheus and Eurydice -- adjacent-real).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Rome's actual founding date (traditionally 753 BCE); theology owns the AENEAS story that Rome later grafted onto its origin. GEOGRAPHY owns the Tiber, Latium, the seven hills as places.

name: The Cyclops Polyphemus: 'Nobody' and the burning stake
scope: The most famous single episode of the Odyssey. T1: sailing home from Troy, ODYSSEUS and TWELVE of his crew land on an island of huge one-eyed shepherd giants -- the CYCLOPES -- and enter the cave of one of them, POLYPHEMUS, son of POSEIDON, hoping for guest-gifts. Instead, the giant rolls a stone across the mouth of the cave that no man could move, and eats TWO of the crew for supper, dashing their brains out against the floor (Odyssey 9.287-293). T2: the next morning Polyphemus eats TWO MORE for breakfast and drives his flocks out to pasture, sealing the cave behind him. Odysseus and his men are trapped -- if they kill the giant in his sleep, they will never move the stone; if they wait, they will be eaten one meal at a time. Odysseus has a plan. He and his men sharpen the giant's great olive-wood staff into a huge STAKE and hide it. T3: when Polyphemus comes back and eats TWO MORE crewmen, Odysseus offers him a skin of very strong WINE. The giant drinks and asks the guest's name to give him his gift. Odysseus answers: 'OUTIS is my name; my mother, my father, my friends call me OUTIS' (Odyssey 9.366-367). OUTIS in Greek means 'NOBODY'. Polyphemus laughs and promises: 'I will eat Nobody LAST, after all his friends' -- and passes out drunk. T4: Odysseus and four men take the sharpened stake, heat its point RED in the fire, and drive it into the giant's SINGLE EYE, twisting it 'as a shipwright bores a beam with a drill' (Odyssey 9.383-388). Polyphemus roars in agony; the other Cyclopes come running to the mouth of the cave and shout 'Polyphemus, who is hurting you?' He roars back: 'NOBODY is killing me! NOBODY, my friends!' -- and they leave, telling him it must be an illness from Zeus. In the morning, Odysseus lashes each of his surviving men to the belly of one of the giant's RAMS and clings to the biggest ram himself. Polyphemus, now blind, feels the backs of the sheep as they pass but not the bellies. T5: safe out at sea, Odysseus makes his one great mistake -- he shouts back his REAL NAME across the water to taunt the blinded giant. Polyphemus prays to his father POSEIDON that Odysseus never reach home, or if he must reach it, that he reach it LATE and ALONE, and find his house in trouble. The god hears. That prayer is the reason the Odyssey is TEN YEARS LONG instead of a short trip. Further rungs: 'Cyclops' means 'round-eye' in Greek (kyklo- + -ops); the OLIVE-WOOD STAKE is a named artifact of the scene; the RAM under which Odysseus escapes is the biggest of the flock, and he addresses a whole speech to it wondering why it comes last today (Odyssey 9.447-460).
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 9.181-566 (whole Cyclops episode: the cave, eating the crew, the wine, 'Outis / Nobody', the stake in the eye, 'as a shipwright bores a beam' 383-388, escape under the rams, Odysseus's taunting name-shout, Polyphemus's prayer to Poseidon). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Polyphemus', 'Odyssey' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia same. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the pun ('OUTIS' vs 'ME TIS' -- 'nobody' vs 'not any') is preserved in the Greek text and worth flagging in context, not the stem.
framing_note: The keystone Odyssey ladder -- must ship. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Odysseus says his name is NOBODY, gets the giant drunk on wine, and when the other giants hear the wounded one screaming 'Nobody is killing me' they walk away) and T4 (they blind the SINGLE eye with a red-hot sharpened stake, then escape by tying themselves to the BELLIES of the giant's rams so the blind giant can only feel wool as his sheep leave the cave). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Nobody' or 'no one' before asking what name Odysseus gave; describe the SCENE (a giant eating crewmen two at a time, a huge stone rolled across a cave mouth, a skin of strong wine, a sharpened stake in the fire) and let the recall be the NAME he gave, the number of EYES, or the method of ESCAPE. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as David and Goliath, or Cuchulainn against the giant Nechtan -- 'the one-eyed giant', 'the great olive-wood stake'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other giants Odysseus meets (Laestrygonians -- next ladder, easy to confuse), other 'give a false name' scenes (Jacob taking Esau's blessing), other 'blinding the giant' or 'trapped in a cave' scenes (Ali Baba, Beowulf under the water in Grendel's mother's hall).
history_overlap: None -- pure Odyssey.

name: Circe of Aeaea: pigs, moly, and the year on the island
scope: The witch of the wandering. T1: driven off course after the Cyclops and the Laestrygonians (who hurl boulders down from the cliffs and destroy eleven of Odysseus's twelve ships, so that only Odysseus's own ship reaches Circe), the survivors land on AEAEA, the island of the enchantress CIRCE, daughter of the Sun and sister of the sorceress who is Medea's aunt. They see smoke rising from a stone house in a forest clearing where wolves and lions -- Circe's transformed former visitors -- fawn like tame dogs. T2: Odysseus sends half his men, led by EURYLOCHUS, to investigate. Circe welcomes them in and gives them a feast laced with a DRUG that makes them forget home; then she touches them one by one with her WAND and TURNS THEM INTO SWINE, driving them out to sty and feeding them acorns. They keep their human minds inside the pig bodies -- and weep. Eurylochus, who has hung back at the door, escapes and runs to warn Odysseus. T3: Odysseus sets out alone to rescue his men. HERMES meets him on the path and gives him an antidote -- the MOLY, a black-rooted white-flowered plant Homer names as 'moly' and says only the gods can pull it up (Odyssey 10.302-306). Hermes tells him exactly what to do: when Circe strikes with the wand and orders him to the sty, DRAW his sword and rush her; she will drop the wand and offer to sleep with him; make her swear a great oath first, that she will do him and his men no more harm. T4: it works exactly as Hermes said. Circe stares -- 'you must be Odysseus of the many turns, Hermes always said you would come to me on your way home from Troy' -- and drops the wand. Odysseus makes her swear the oath. She then turns his men back from pigs to men (larger and younger and handsomer than before), and welcomes the whole crew, and they stay a YEAR on her island in her feast-hall. T5: at the end of the year the crew persuades Odysseus that it is time to sail. Before he can go home, Circe tells him, he must first sail DOWN to the underworld to consult the blind seer TIRESIAS about the way home (next topic). She gives him the ram-and-ewe he will need for the offering, and the wind for the sail, and sends him on. Further rungs: her father is the Sun (HELIOS) -- the same god whose cattle on Thrinacia will destroy the rest of the crew later; her name in Greek gives us 'circean' for anything that traps and transforms; the MOLY is one of the few named-and-specified plants in Homer, and its identification (some scholars have proposed snowdrop, some mandrake, some a purely mythical plant) is still debated.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 10.133-574 (whole Circe episode: the wolves and lions, Eurylochus and the pigs, Hermes and the moly plant, the oath, the year at the feast-hall, the instructions to sail to Hades); Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.244-307 (the Latin retelling with more moralizing). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Circe', 'Odyssey' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia 'Circe', 'Moly (herb)'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the description of moly at Odyssey 10.302-306 ('black at the root but with a flower like milk') -- lock the Lattimore wording; the identification of the plant is famously unsettled and should be flagged in context, not stem.
framing_note: The keystone WITCH ladder of the Odyssey and the setup for the descent to Hades. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (she turns the crewmen into PIGS with a wand and drug, and the men keep their human MINDS inside the pig bodies) and T3 (HERMES gives Odysseus a MAGIC PLANT called moly as the antidote to her drugs -- Homer NAMES it and describes it 'black at the root, white flower'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'pigs' before asking what Circe did to the crew; describe the SCENE (a witch's stone house in a forest, tame wolves and lions in the yard, a feast, a wand) and let the recall be the animal (PIGS specifically, not wolves), the PLANT Hermes gives, or the OATH Odysseus makes her swear. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the sorceress Freyja teaching Odin seidr, or Morgan le Fay in an Arthurian romance -- 'the witch of Aeaea', 'the god Hermes on the path'. No 'evil sorceress' judgment -- she becomes an ally within one scene. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Odyssey enchantresses (CALYPSO on Ogygia, who keeps him seven years; the SIRENS' voice; NAUSICAA's mother Arete), other 'turn into animals' scenes (Actaeon into a stag, Callisto into a bear), other named magic plants (nepenthe -- also Homer, in Odyssey 4 at Helen's table; mandrake; the golden bough of Aeneid 6).
history_overlap: None -- pure Odyssey.

name: The descent to Hades: Tiresias, Odysseus's mother, and the shades
scope: Odyssey 11 -- the Nekuia, the summoning of the dead. T1: on Circe's instructions ODYSSEUS sails to the far edge of the world where the RIVER OCEAN meets the entrance to the underworld. He digs a pit, pours libations of milk, honey, wine and water into it, and cuts the throats of a black RAM and a black EWE so that their blood pools in the trench -- the shades of the dead cannot speak until they have drunk BLOOD. T2: the first shade to come is ELPENOR, the youngest crewman, who had drunkenly fallen off the ROOF of Circe's palace and broken his neck the night before they sailed and whom they had left UNBURIED. He begs Odysseus to go back to Aeaea and give him proper burial, and to plant his OAR upright as a grave-marker on the beach. T3: then comes the shade of the blind SEER TIRESIAS of Thebes -- the reason for the whole journey. Drinking the blood, Tiresias prophesies: Odysseus WILL reach home, but only after long trouble; on the way he will pass THRINACIA where the CATTLE OF THE SUN graze -- if he or his men touch a single beast, the men will die and Odysseus will reach home alone and late and find his house full of arrogant suitors; and even after that, Odysseus must one day take an OAR inland from Ithaca until he meets a man who mistakes it for a WINNOWING FAN, and there plant the oar and sacrifice to Poseidon (Odyssey 11.121-137). T4: after Tiresias comes Odysseus's own MOTHER, ANTICLEIA. She had been alive when he left for Troy. He tries three times to embrace her and three times his arms pass through her 'like a shadow or a dream' (Odyssey 11.204-208, Lattimore). She tells him she died of GRIEF waiting for him. T5: then a long parade of famous shades comes to the pit and drinks the blood in turn: AGAMEMNON, who tells the story of his own murder by his wife Clytemnestra in the bath the moment he came home from Troy and warns Odysseus never to trust a woman completely; ACHILLES, who says the famous line -- 'I would rather be a hired servant of a poor man on the earth than king over all the dead' (Odyssey 11.489-491, Lattimore); AJAX THE GREAT, who turns his back and walks away in silence, still angry over the armor; and the ancient sinners in torment -- TITYUS with the vultures eating his liver, TANTALUS in water and fruit he can never reach (whence 'tantalize'), SISYPHUS forever rolling his stone up a hill only to have it roll down. Odysseus flees when he begins to fear the head of the Gorgon MEDUSA will be sent up next. Further rungs: this WHOLE-BOOK descent is the model for every later 'katabasis' scene in Western literature -- Aeneid 6 (Aeneas and the golden bough), Dante's Inferno (Virgil as guide, opening with a katabasis from Homer's), the harrowing of Hell in Christian legend.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 11 (whole book: the pit, the blood, Elpenor and the oar, Tiresias's prophecy including the cattle of the Sun and the far-inland oar 121-137, Anticleia and the three failed embraces 204-208, Agamemnon, Achilles's 'hired servant' line 489-491, Ajax the silent shade, Tityus / Tantalus / Sisyphus). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Nekuia', 'Odyssey', 'Tiresias' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia 'Nekyia', 'Katabasis'. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Achilles's 'I would rather be a hired servant' -- verify Lattimore vs Fagles wording ('I would rather follow the plow as thrall to another man' vs 'By god, I'd rather slave on earth for another man'). Both usable.
framing_note: The keystone descent-to-the-dead ladder of the strand. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (Odysseus tries THREE TIMES to embrace his dead mother and her body passes through his arms like a shadow) and T5 (ACHILLES, the greatest hero of the Iliad, says he would rather be a HIRED SERVANT of a poor man ALIVE than KING over all the dead -- the man who chose glory over long life now saying he chose wrong). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Tiresias' before asking whose prophecy Odysseus went down to hear; describe the SCENE (a pit at the edge of the world, black rams and ewes bled into it, shades of the dead crowding for the blood) and let the recall be the SEER's name, the first shade to come (ELPENOR), or Achilles's famous line. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Christ's harrowing of Hell, or Odin at Mimir's well, or the Volva raised from the dead in the Voluspa -- 'the pit at the world's edge', 'the shade of the mother'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other underworld journeys (Orpheus for Eurydice, Aeneas in Aeneid 6, the harrowing of Hell in Christian tradition, Persephone's descent), other Homer prophecies (Calchas at Aulis, Cassandra), other 'famous shades' (which souls Odysseus meets vs which Aeneas meets in the parallel Aeneid 6 scene).
history_overlap: None. Note: the harrowing of Hell (Christian strand) is a cousin katabasis worth cross-referencing but keep specifics distinct.

name: The Sirens: the mast and the wax
scope: The most famous 'don't listen' scene in the West. T1: CIRCE, before letting Odysseus leave her island, warns him that on the next leg of his journey he will pass a meadow-strand where the SIRENS sit and sing to sailors -- women (or in early art, bird-bodied women) whose song is so beautiful that any sailor who hears it steers his ship onto the rocks, and the shore around them is white with the bones of the men their song has drawn to death. T2: Circe gives him the precise counter-trick. He is to soften a lump of BEESWAX in the sun, knead it, and PLUG THE EARS of every man in the crew so they cannot hear at all. He himself, though, may LISTEN -- if he wishes -- but only if his crew ties him standing upright to the MAST of the ship, hand and foot, with orders that if he begs them to release him they must LASH HIM TIGHTER, not free him. T3: they do exactly this. Odysseus, alone of all men in the story, hears the Sirens' song and lives -- he ties his crew's ears with wax, is bound to the mast, and orders them not to obey his signals. The Sirens sing to him personally, calling him by name, offering to tell him ALL the things that happened at Troy and ALL the things that will yet happen on the earth. In Homer their song is one of KNOWLEDGE, not (as often popularly imagined) of sex -- they promise omniscient understanding. T4: Odysseus, hearing it, THRASHES against his bonds and SCREAMS at his men to release him, throwing his eyebrows up as a signal; two of them, PERIMEDES and EURYLOCHUS, get up and TIGHTEN his ropes just as he told them to. The ship passes; the wax comes out of the ears; the mast-bindings are cut; the crew is safe (Odyssey 12.165-200). T5: the Sirens are Homer's picture of a temptation that ONLY works if you can hear it -- knowledge you would die to have. The scene is the origin of the English idiom 'a siren song' for a beautiful lure toward disaster; it is set to music in Debussy, painted by Waterhouse (1891, National Gallery of Victoria), and reworked by Kafka in his tiny parable 'The Silence of the Sirens' (where Odysseus's real trick is that he pretends not to notice that they don't actually sing). Further rungs: Homer says only TWO Sirens (Odyssey 12.52 -- 'two Sirens', ambiguous); later Greek writers count THREE and name them (Parthenope, Ligeia, Leucosia); the earliest Greek vase-paintings show them as BIRD-BODIED with human heads, the medieval and Renaissance ones as FISH-tailed mermaids.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 12.39-54 (Circe's warning) and 12.165-200 (the passage: wax, mast, tightening the ropes, Perimedes and Eurylochus). Lattimore and Fagles standard English. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Sirens', 'Odyssey' (403; via browser 2026-09-04); Wikipedia 'Siren (mythology)'. Also relevant: Kafka, 'Das Schweigen der Sirenen'; Waterhouse painting 'Ulysses and the Sirens' 1891. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: 'the shore white with bones' -- verify Lattimore Odyssey 12.45.
framing_note: The neat mirror-pair to the Cyclops (cleverness against a fatal charm). Dinner-test payoff: T2-T3 (beeswax in the ears of the crew, Odysseus TIED to the MAST -- alone of all men he HEARS the Sirens and lives, but he screams to be released and his crew has orders to tighten the ropes) and T3 (in Homer the Sirens promise KNOWLEDGE, not sex -- they offer to tell him everything that happened at Troy and everything that will happen on earth). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'mast' before asking what Odysseus did to hear the Sirens; describe the SCENE (a strand white with the bones of dead sailors, a beautiful song, a crew whose ears are stopped, one man who wants to hear) and let the recall be the exact TECHNIQUE (mast + wax, split between him and the crew), the SUBSTANCE (beeswax), or the two crewmen who tighten the ropes. HISTORICAL vs LEGENDARY: pure Homer, though the specific two-vs-three count and the bird-vs-fish body come from later art. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as Loki tying himself under the venom-drip on Sigyn's bowl, or Cuchulainn's ristrad in the wagon -- 'the beautiful and deadly song', 'the beeswax and the mast'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other 'temptation you have to endure' scenes (Christ in the wilderness -- Christian-strand distractor; Buddha under the Bodhi -- non-Western, out), other Odyssey female voices (Circe, Calypso, the Sirens, Nausicaa, Penelope -- careful about who is who), other 'plug the ears' folk motifs.
history_overlap: None -- pure Homer.

name: Scylla and Charybdis: six heads and a whirlpool
scope: The two-fold monster-strait of Homer. T1: the same warning-speech Circe gives Odysseus about the Sirens also warns him about the NEXT hazard: a narrow strait with cliffs on both sides, in which two monsters wait, and no ship can avoid both. On one cliff lives SCYLLA. On the other -- 'within a bowshot' (Odyssey 12.101) -- lurks CHARYBDIS. T2: CHARYBDIS is a WHIRLPOOL. Three times a day she sucks down the black seawater in a huge spinning funnel that drags a ship straight to the bottom; three times a day she spits it back up. No ship caught in her draw survives -- 'not even Poseidon could save you' (Odyssey 12.107). T3: SCYLLA is a monster growing out of the OPPOSITE cliff: SIX long serpent-necks with SIX dog-fanged HEADS, each with three rows of teeth, and TWELVE feet; she reaches down from her cave and each of the six heads snatches ONE MAN off a passing ship. There is no way to fight her -- as long as it takes to hurl a spear, six sailors are gone. T4: Circe tells Odysseus the choice honestly: he must sail CLOSER to Scylla, because she will only take SIX of his men, but Charybdis will take EVERYTHING. He does. As they pass, Scylla's six heads snatch SIX crewmen, and as they die 'they called on my name, and I saw them lifted, and lifted still' (Odyssey 12.245-259, Lattimore -- 'this was the most pitiful thing my eyes have seen of all my wanderings'). T5: 'between Scylla and Charybdis' is the origin of the English idiom for an unavoidable choice between two bad options (equivalent 'between a rock and a hard place'). Odyssey 12 says the strait is at the edge of the world; later Greek and Roman writers, from Thucydides to Virgil to Pliny, IDENTIFY it with the STRAIT OF MESSINA between Sicily and mainland Italy -- Scylla on the Italian cliff (the town of SCILLA in Calabria takes its name from her), Charybdis on the Sicilian side. Further rungs: after the disaster on Thrinacia (next topic) Odysseus is later swept BACK through the strait ALONE -- clinging to the FIG TREE growing from the cliff over Charybdis's mouth, hanging like a bat as his raft is sucked down and waiting for her to spit the raft back up so he can drop onto it (Odyssey 12.431-446); this is one of the most vivid single images in the whole poem.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Odyssey 12.73-126 (Circe's warning), 12.201-259 (the passage: Scylla takes six, the pitiful voices), 12.431-446 (Odysseus later clinging to the fig tree over Charybdis).
